summary: In the present tense Hebrew has no verb “to be”: the subject and what it is simply stand side by side — אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט “I (am) a student”, הַמּוֹרֶה פֹּה “the teacher (is) here”. This is a nominal sentence. In the past and future the verb הָיָה appears and agrees with the subject: הוּא הָיָה מוֹרֶה “he was a teacher”, הִיא הָיְתָה סְטוּדֶנְטִית, הֵם הָיוּ חֲבֵרִים; הוּא יִהְיֶה / הִיא תִּהְיֶה “he / she will be”. Between two nouns, especially in definitions, a pronoun that agrees with the subject can stand where “is” would be: יֶלֶד הוּא אָדָם “a child is a person”.

items.title: Present — no verb
points: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט — I am a student
הִיא מוֹרָה — she is a teacher
הַסֵּפֶר פֹּה — the book is here
זֶה בַּיִת — this is a house

items.title: Past and future — הָיָה
points: אֲנִי הָיִיתִי סְטוּדֶנְט — I was a student
הִיא הָיְתָה מוֹרָה — she was a teacher
הַסֵּפֶר הָיָה פֹּה — the book was here
הִיא תִּהְיֶה מוֹרָה — she will be a teacher

head: past
future
blocks.caption: The forms of הָיָה you meet now (the rest of the future comes with the verb lessons). Everyday spelling of הָיְתָה: הייתה.

blocks.text: The order is subject first, then the predicate. In the past the verb goes between them: הַמּוֹרָה הָיְתָה פֹּה.

blocks.title: Agreement in the past
blocks.text: הָיָה agrees with the subject, not with the noun after it: הַמִּטָּה הָיְתָה שָׁם (מִטָּה is feminine), הַשֻּׁלְחָן הָיָה פֹּה, הַסְּפָרִים הָיוּ פֹּה.

blocks.title: Do not invent a present
blocks.text: There is no *אֲנִי הוֹוֶה סְטוּדֶנְט and no *אֲנִי הָיָה סְטוּדֶנְט for “I am”. הָיָה is always past: “was”.

blocks.title: The pronoun as “is”
blocks.text: With a noun subject, especially in definitions, Hebrew can put הוּא / הִיא / הֵם / הֵן where a linking “is / are” would stand: יֶלֶד הוּא אָדָם, יְלָדִים הֵם אֲנָשִׁים. It agrees with the subject. With a pronoun subject it is not used: אֲנִי מוֹרֶה, never *אֲנִי הוּא מוֹרֶה.

blocks.title: Ask yourself
questions: Was it, or will it be? → a form of הָיָה.
Who or what is the subject: masculine, feminine, plural?

askYourself: Is the sentence about now? → no verb at all: subject + noun / place.
Is it about the past? → הָיָה in the form of the subject: הָיִיתִי, הָיָה, הָיְתָה, הָיוּ …
Is it about the future? → יִהְיֶה (he), תִּהְיֶה (she), אֶהְיֶה (I) …
What is the gender and number of the subject? The verb follows the subject, not the noun after it.
Is the subject a noun and the predicate a noun, as in a definition? → you may add הוּא / הִיא / הֵם / הֵן (agreeing with the subject).
Is it “there is / there are”? → that is יֵשׁ (lesson 6), not a form of הָיָה in the present.
steps: Decide the time: present, past or future.
Present: put the subject and the predicate side by side.
Past or future: insert the form of הָיָה that agrees with the subject.

traps: No present “to be”: אֲנִי מוֹרֶה, not *אֲנִי הוּא מוֹרֶה or *אֲנִי הָיָה מוֹרֶה.
Past agreement follows the subject: הַדֶּלֶת הָיְתָה שָׁם (feminine), not *הַדֶּלֶת הָיָה שָׁם.
In the past the pronoun can be dropped (הָיִיתִי סְטוּדֶנְט), in the present it cannot (אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט).
The pronoun copula agrees with the subject, not with the predicate: אִשָּׁה הִיא אָדָם (אִשָּׁה is feminine, although אָדָם is masculine).

seeAlso.note: Arabic too has a verbless present (أَنَا طَالِبٌ “I (am) a student”) and uses كَانَ in the past — which, unlike Hebrew הָיָה, puts the predicate in the accusative.
German always says the verb and conjugates it for person: ich bin, du bist, er ist — Hebrew says nothing in the present.
Chinese 是 links two nouns (我是学生) but is not used before adjectives (他很高); Hebrew needs no linking word for either.

notes.text: Russian too has no “is” in the present and a gendered past: я студент — он был учителем — она была студенткой; Hebrew אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט — הוּא הָיָה מוֹרֶה — הִיא הָיְתָה סְטוּדֶנְטִית. One difference: the noun after הָיָה keeps its form (no instrumental like учителем).
Arabic also leaves the verb out in the present (أَنَا طَالِبٌ) and uses كَانَ in the past; but كَانَ puts its predicate in the accusative (كَانَ طَالِبًا), while the noun after הָיָה never changes.
English always says am / is / are; the Hebrew present has no verb at all: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט “I (am) a student”. Do not translate “is” with הוּא after a pronoun.
German conjugates sein in every tense (ich bin, du bist, er ist); Hebrew is silent in the present and says הָיָה / יִהְיֶה only in the past and future.
Greek always uses είμαι (είμαι φοιτητής); Hebrew drops it in the present. Like ήταν, הָיָה agrees with the subject — and in Hebrew also in gender: הָיָה / הָיְתָה.

Spanish splits “to be” into ser and estar; in the Hebrew present both are missing — אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט (soy estudiante) and הַסֵּפֶר פֹּה (el libro está aquí) are both verbless, and in the past both are הָיָה.
French always uses être (je suis étudiant); Hebrew says nothing in the present. In the past הָיָה agrees with the subject in gender as well: הוּא הָיָה / הִיא הָיְתָה.
Hindi closes the sentence with a form of होना (मैं छात्र हूँ); Hebrew has no present copula and nothing at the end: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט.
Persian always adds “to be”, as a word or an ending (دانشجو هستم / دانشجوام); Hebrew adds nothing in the present.
Marathi always has आहे (मी विद्यार्थी आहे “I am a student”); the Hebrew present has no copula at all.

Turkish has no separate verb in the present either, but it adds personal endings to the predicate (öğrenciyim “I am a student”); Hebrew adds nothing: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט. For the past Turkish adds -di (öğrenciydim); Hebrew uses the verb הָיָה.
Japanese closes the sentence with です / だ (学生です); Hebrew has no copula in the present, and in the past הָיָה stands between the subject and the predicate.
Korean attaches the copula -이다 to the noun (학생이에요); Hebrew attaches nothing in the present.
Finnish always says olla (minä olen opiskelija); in Hebrew the present is verbless.
Hungarian also drops van in the third person present (ő tanár “he is a teacher”) but keeps vagyok, vagy … for “I, you”; Hebrew drops the verb in every person: אֲנִי מוֹרֶה, אַתָּה מוֹרֶה.
Swahili links two nouns with ni (mimi ni mwanafunzi); Hebrew needs no linking word — only the optional pronoun הוּא / הִיא between two nouns (יֶלֶד הוּא אָדָם) works a little like ni.
Chinese 是 links two nouns (我是学生) but is left out before adjectives (他很高); Hebrew uses no linking word for either: אֲנִי סְטוּדֶנְט, הוּא גָּבֹהַּ.
Vietnamese puts là between two nouns (tôi là sinh viên) but not before adjectives; Hebrew uses no linking word for either.
Inuktitut turns the noun itself into a verb with a suffix and a personal ending (“I-am-a-teacher” in one word); Hebrew leaves the noun as it is and adds nothing in the present.
